h1: Scaling a gin brand from hundreds to thousands of cases
title: Scaling a Gin Brand | Craft Beer School
desc: What changes when a gin brand grows: capacity, working capital, quality control, people, distribution and the choice between contract and own production.
teaser: Growth breaks things that worked at small scale. Plan the stages before the orders arrive.
standfirst: Selling hundreds of cases is a craft. Selling thousands is an operation. The change shows up in cash, quality and people before it shows up in profit.
sections:
A case is a standard shipping unit, often six or twelve bottles. At a few hundred cases a year, a founder can make, fill, sell and deliver. At several thousand, no single person can do it all.

The product has to stay the same while the business changes around it. Drinkers do not care about your growth. They care that the gin tastes as it did.

Quality problems grow with volume. Botanical lots vary, batches overlap and fatigue sets in. Put the routine in writing before you need it: goods-in checks, a recipe sheet, hearts cut points, strength checks, a retained sample from every batch and a release decision that someone owns.

In quality work we often see small producers rely on one person's palate. That works until that person is away. Train a second taster and keep reference samples. See sourcing botanicals commercially and buying neutral spirit for gin for supplier control.

Revisit your capacity plan. The bottleneck at 500 cases is rarely the bottleneck at 5,000. Time each step again. You may need a faster filler, more tanks, more storage or a second shift before you need a larger still. Use production capacity planning as the method.

Decide whether more volume comes from your own plant, a larger contract or both.

Growth consumes cash. You buy more spirit, glass and botanicals before the sale. Your customers pay later. A hypothetical illustration: if sales double and you are paid in 60 days while paying suppliers in 30, you need to fund about a month of extra turnover. A profitable brand can run out of cash this way.

Build a cash flow that shows the working capital for each growth step. Review it monthly. Talk to lenders and investors before the need becomes urgent. See funding a gin brand.

Plan who does what as you grow: production, quality, sales, accounts, compliance. Write down the routines that live in a founder's head. Use simple systems for stock, batch records, orders and invoices. A shared spreadsheet may do at first. A proper system may be worth it later.

Compliance grows with volume too. More stock, more movement and more states or countries mean more records and returns.

More outlets are not always better. Look at which accounts reorder, which distributors push you and where you earn the best margin. Sell more where it works before opening new territory. Keep price discipline as you grow, because discounts tend to spread.
Make versus buy and the data to track

At some point you will ask whether to build capacity or rent it. Make a fresh comparison using current volumes and current quotes. Contract capacity may look dearer per bottle but needs little capital. Your own still may look cheaper but needs staff, space and licences. The answer can change as volume grows. A mix is often sensible. The earlier comparison is in distil it yourself or contract it.

Growth needs numbers on one page: bottles produced, bottles sold, stock on hand, yield from spirit to bottle, cost per bottle, margin by account, receivables and cash. Review them monthly. A founder who sees yield slip from one batch to the next can fix it before it costs a season. Quality, cost and data are linked. A simple dashboard beats a clever one that nobody updates.

A distributor who handled ten accounts for you may struggle with a hundred. Check delivery times, stock levels at their warehouse and how often they visit outlets. Ask them to share sales data by account. If they will not, you are selling blind.

At larger volume you may add distributors in new states or countries. Set clear territories and targets. Review them yearly. Be ready to change a partner who does not perform. Write termination terms into the agreement from the start, since they are hard to add later.

Many producers need an outside review of the whole operation when they grow. We carry out reviews of cost, quality and data. We also help with contract manufacturing arrangements. The work can be done remotely or on site by arrangement.
faqs: When should I move from contract to my own still?
When your volume, cash and plan show that owning the plant would lower cost or give control you need. Compare both at your real volume.
What breaks first as volume rises?
Often cash, then quality control and then people. Check all three early.
How do I keep the gin consistent?
Use written recipes, reference samples, supplier specifications and a clear release decision.
Should I add new products to grow?
Only after the core sells well. More products add stock and complexity.
